news.title: A homecoming for “A Different World”
news.text:
Five episodes into Netflix’s “A Different World” sequel, Hillman gets a bomb threat. This is a very real part of life for students at historically black colleges and universities, but that doesn’t make it any less frightening. Everyone gathers at The Pit, including Dwayne Wayne (Kadeem Hardison) and Freddie Brooks (Cree Summer) — who are Hillman faculty now — to talk it out. One student expresses shock at being targeted at a place they chose because they thought they’d feel safe. Another wonders if it’s an inside job.

The person who best sums up the moment is Dwayne’s daughter, Deborah (Maleah Joi Moon), when she says, “It’s all so exhausting. We go to their institutions, they punish us. We try to build our own; they destroy it. We mess up, they use it against us. What is even the point of trying?”

Right now, that statement could and will be read any number of ways.

There’s the threat itself, which echoes similar ones against HBCUs in the wake of Charlie Kirk’s shooting last September. It also recalls 2022, when more than 30 HBCUs were hit with comparable incidents between January and mid-March.

Deborah could just as easily be critiquing the Trump administration’s vacillation between defunding educational opportunities for minority students, citing the DEI boogeyman, and infusing HBCUs and tribal colleges with millions in cash. Great for those higher-learning institutions, but targeting minority grant funding elsewhere ensures, particularly at the Ivies and Big 10 schools, less diverse undergraduate populations at places that weren’t racially or economically diverse in the first place.

To know “A Different World” as it was is to anticipate that this 2026 visit to Hillman, a fictional HBCU, must contend with these real-world concerns. But, returning to the episode in question, what’s just as vital is how its students deal with this crisis. When the waiting becomes almost too much, Deborah starts humming a few bars of a familiar song. More join in, and soon everybody is singing along, dropping the tension enough to relax a little.

A few breaths later, the lockdown ends. Everyone resumes their business, carrying with them the lesson of never sacrificing their spirit even while living in a state of constant vigilance.

Expecting the modern, single-camera version of “A Different World” to recapture the multi-camera original’s magic is unreasonable. Read the title, read the room. The 2026 version of “A Different World” comes to us not on a traditional broadcast network, but on a streaming service, where Norman Lear’s return to “One Day at a Time” became a loving chronicle of a Cuban American family’s life. It also adapted Justin Simien’s indie flick “Dear White People” into an in-your-face comedy revolving around the Black experience at an Ivy League college.

But that show relied on the specter of white ignorance to serve as a cultural contrast, whereas “A Different World” is, as the title promises, almost entirely centered on Blackness – and with it, Black joy.

(Eli Joshua Ade/Netflix © 2026)

To those wondering what this show has to contribute 39 years after its 1987 premiere, and following the returns of “Roseanne” and “Will & Grace,” “Full House,” and “That ‘70s Show” (reborn as “That ’90s Show“), that should be enough.

Presumably, explaining Black college life to an audience that almost elected Howard graduate Kamala Harris to our nation’s highest office — and that views her fellow alumnus Ta-Nehisi Coates as one of Black America’s representative voices — is less of a requirement these days. 

Even so, “A Different World,” being a spinoff of “The Cosby Show,” faced different backroom hurdles before its executive producer Debbie Allen got her long-sought greenlight. The holdup is precisely what you think it is. Although Allen and the original series’ head writer, Susan Fales-Hill, shaped the show into the version considered a sitcom classic, Bill Cosby’s creator credit tainted its reputation. The comedian is accused of sexually assaulting dozens of women and was convicted in 2018. That conviction was overturned in 2021 because of a non-prosecution agreement struck with a previous prosecutor. (Cosby continues to maintain his innocence.)

Now that it’s back and under the guidance of “Grey’s Anatomy” alumna Felicia Pride, I can almost guarantee there will be right-wing media commentators crowing, “Who’s they?” while trying to paint this sequel as an extra-woke version of the original.

Doing that would betray their ignorance of the show’s legacy, especially the five seasons that Allen captained. At a time when other sitcoms occasionally tackled social issues in “very special” episodes and “The Cosby Show” hewed to its namesake star’s dedication to respectability politics, “A Different World” regularly confronted harder topics.

Author and professor Brittney Cooper explains what that means in a 2013 Salon story, where she remembers Dr. Huxtable’s eldest daughter Sondra naming her adorable twins Winnie and Nelson after anti-apartheid revolutionaries Winnie and Nelson Mandela in 1988, when they were mainstream political celebrities. Two years later, Hillman student Kimberly Reese (Charnele Brown) agonized over whether to reject a scholarship funded by a company linked to South Africa’s apartheid regime, which was a political act.

None of it felt forced to anyone who sees the college experience as one of political and social awakening. But even “A Different World” hit its limits when it plunged the audience inside the Black folks’ shock and despair after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising. That decision likely led NBC to yank the plug despite its high ratings, Fales-Hill admitted to Vanity Fair. It’s easy to say that was a different time, except we know that isn’t true.

On the contrary, this return to “A Different World” simultaneously reminds us of how far TV has regressed since the late ‘80s and early ‘90s. The original’s success paved the way for a surge in shows centering Black life in America, including “Living Single,” “Moesha” and “Martin.” It also brought HBCU culture and traditions like step competitions into Middle America’s living rooms.

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last.
Sign up here 

Still, this generation of “A Different World” viewers needs to be spoken to in ways beyond the cultural lingua franca of online posting and situationships, which the first season does well. Deborah Wayne and Ron’s son Shaquille (Cornell Young IV) are in one of those, following in the footsteps of Dwayne and Whitley. But under the constant watch of phone cameras and gossip that travels at the speed of social media feeds, they face greater pressures.

(Daniel Delgado Jr/Netflix © 2026)

Within that on-again-off-again tension crackles an exuberance reflected in the whole ensemble, an array of determined smiles and easy joking that momentarily pushes aside those ever-present societal shadows — including the very real possibility that Hillman might close. 

But as Freddie points out to her students, that cliff has always been there. “Black learning spaces have always been seen as dangerous,” she tells her students, “not just because of what students do, but because of who you might become.” Maintaining their joy, then, is seen as both an educational priority and an act of resistance. That’s worth reviving, too.

“A Different World” is streaming on Netflix.
news.summary: Netflix's anticipated revival prioritizes Black joy at a time when HBCUs and other universities have been targeted
news.author: Melanie McFarland

news.title: Gun Rights Groups Slap Maryland Glock Ban With New Court Filing
news.text:
Pro-Second Amendment groups urged a federal judge Tuesday to grant an injunction blocking Maryland’s ban on Glock pistols.

Hours after Democratic Maryland Gov. Wes Moore signed legislation in May that could ban the sale of Glock pistols, pro-Second Amendment organizations announced they would file suit to have the law thrown out as unconstitutional. In a response filed with the United States District Court for the District of Maryland, the Firearms Policy Coalition (FPC), National Rifle Association (NRA) and Second Amendment Foundation (SAF) said that there was no historical basis to ban firearms because criminals illegally modified them. (RELATED: Gun Manufacturer Slaps Blue State With Suit Over Gun Ban)

FPC announced today that it filed its reply brief in support of a preliminary injunction in Bathras v. Moore, urging the court block Maryland’s new ban on Glock and Glock-style handguns before it takes effect. https://t.co/vXL86UlyjZ— Firearms Policy Coalition (@gunpolicy) September 22, 2026

“The Glock-style handguns that are the target of Maryland’s ban are, by the State’s own admission, not dangerous or unusual arms, but common and ordinary semiautomatic handguns that can be, if illegally modified, converted into machineguns,” the document states. “But there is no history of restricting common arms that could be illegally misused or modified. And there similarly is no history of prohibiting the commercial or private sale of firearms that citizens are constitutionally entitled to possess.”

Under current federal law, it is illegal to possess or manufacture a fully-automatic firearm that is not registered or authorized under the provisions of the National Firearms Act. A conviction for violating the law can lead to up to ten years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

Glock pistols are among the most popular in the United States, regularly appearing in lists of the most-sold firearms compiled by outlets like Guns and Guns and Ammo magazine. The company’s Glock 19X sold over 100,000 copies in less than six months after the pistol’s release, according to a 2018 press release by the company.

In addition to being popular among law-abiding citizens, Glock pistols are also used by numerous law enforcement agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), which has issued versions of the handgun to its agents since 1997. Former Vice President Kamala Harris boasted on multiple occasions about owning a Glock pistol she acquired for personal protection.
news.summary: ‘Not dangerous or unusual arms’

news.title: As GOP revives anti-trans playbook, Dems try to turn the page
news.text:
Republicans are returning to a familiar 2024 playbook in the final weeks before the midterms, stoking fears about transgender people in sports, schools and beyond. 

But this time, Democrats are striking back. Some candidates running in red states have tried to distance themselves from their party’s commitment to transgender rights. Others have taken a different approach, dismissing GOP attacks as a ploy to distract voters from the sputtering economy.

President Donald Trump has called denouncing trans athletes one of Republicans’ greatest “soundbites of all time all time” — and a strategy he wants to keep in reserve as November nears with control of Congress on the line.

“I don’t like to do it much before the election. I like to wait,” he said at this month’s GOP convention, because he is “petrified” that Democrats will change their messaging and say, “You know what? Men should not be playing in women’s sports.” 

“And that will really hurt us,” Trump said.

Support for trans athletes has emerged as a growing fault line within the Democratic Party. While the number in high school or college interscholastic sports is vanishingly small, a Pew Research Center survey last year found that 73 percent of Americans were uncomfortable with the idea of athletes competing on teams that don’t match their sex at birth.

Democrats across the ideological spectrum, from California Gov. Gavin Newsom to House candidates running in battleground districts to Senate candidates competing in purple-shaded states, are seeking to reframe the issue.

“Boys should not play in girls’ sports,’’ Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur, who is running for a 23rd term in a northwest Ohio battleground that grew a shade redder after recent redistricting, said in a new ad.

Her stance drew a sharp response from some Democratic leaders in Toledo, who objected to Kaptur’s “hurtful language,” including expressing her opposition to “transgender ideology,” mimicking a phrase used by Republicans.

“This is the type of harmful ad we expect from Derek Merrin and the Republicans,’’ the Lucas County Democratic Party wrote in a social media post, referring to the GOP candidate running against Kaptur. The group noted that it has asked Kaptur’s campaign to take down the ad.

Blake Gendebien, a farmer running for retiring GOP Rep. Elise Stefanik’s seat in New York’s North Country, used similar language in a recent ad. “I served on the school board and coached JV basketball,’’ he said. “I’ve always been clear, boys shouldn’t play on girls’ sports teams.”

And Sarah Trone Garriott, a state senator and an ordained Lutheran minister running against Republican Rep. Zach Nunn in Iowa, ran an ad saying she opposes “letting men in women’s locker rooms” and voted in the legislature “to let parents, not politicians, make decisions for their kids.”

Rep. Mark Takano, who co-chairs Equality PAC, the political arm of the Congressional Equality Caucus, acknowledged the political realities that some battleground Democrats face.

“We recognize that no member will agree with us on every vote, and that is part of the legislative process,’’ the California Democrat said in an emailed statement. “It is imperative that we continue to welcome ‘imperfect allies’ to facilitate meaningful and lasting change for the LGBTQ community.”

But, he added, “there is a clear line: we will not accept candidates or members using Republican rhetoric that actively harms members of our community — particularly transgender Americans, who have been the target of sustained attacks from the Trump Administration.”

Tyler Hack, executive director of the Christopher Street Project, which backs candidates that support trans rights, said the sports question is “a wedge issue manufactured” by Republicans. 

“This is how they start rolling back all of our rights,’’ Hack said. “They started with a restriction that was most politically feasible and most popular among voters. … The fact is, Trump and his cronies have spoken very clearly that they want to eradicate transgenderism.”

Party priorities

The issue has also reemerged in several Senate competitive races — and a hearing on Capitol Hill this week provided fresh fodder.

“The Democrats are choosing to let their two witnesses’ seats go empty. That says a lot,” Judiciary Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, said as he accused his colleagues of blowing off the hearing, titled “Standing Up for Women in Sports.” 

Sen. Darline Graham, a Republican member of the Judiciary panel who is facing an unexpectedly robust challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina, seized on the occasion. Her campaign issued a press release Wednesday highlighting her participation in the hearing and Andrews’ previous social media posts on the topic, calling her a “flip-flop queen.” 

“I am a volleyball mom and proud defender of women’s athletics,” Graham said. “Unfortunately, my opponent is not.”

At the hearing, Judiciary ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., called for “honesty and compassion” around the topic while simultaneously trying to neutralize it. 

“If you ask the American people, ‘What are the priority issues you hope Congress will address as soon as possible?’ the issue of this hearing would not be in the top 10, maybe not the top 20,” he said.

That dynamic has played out on the campaign trail as Senate Democrats look to expand the map and compete in unexpected places. They need a net gain of four seats to retake the chamber. 

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico struck a note of regret for past comments about God being “nonbinary,” playing defense as opponent Ken Paxton ran an ad featuring an AI-generated Talarico reciting his previous remarks on gender identity and religion. Outside groups have also dusted off a phrase Trump deployed against Kamala Harris in 2024 — accusing the Texas Democrat of being “for they/them, not you.”

“What I was trying to say is that you can’t use human categories to define God,” Talarico explained during a Fox News interview, adding he would oppose trans student-athletes competing in girls’ sports “if it endangers safety or fairness.”

But he also tried moving from defense to offense, saying the reason Republicans “want to talk about six sexes is because they don’t want to talk about $6 diesel.”

Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown is making a similar play in his comeback bid against GOP Sen. Jon Husted, accusing Republicans of seeking to deflect attention away from the war in Iran and the rising cost of living.

“With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” a voter says in a recent Brown ad, while another observes that “in Ohio, it’s against the law to perform transgender surgeries on kids. That’s right, it’s illegal.” 

“Jon Husted, why don’t you start working for us?” voters ask in the ad.

Some Democrats have opted for a more nuanced approach. Lindsay James, an Iowa state lawmaker running in an open battleground seat, called for “common sense rules to keep sports fair.” But James, a Presbyterian minister, noted that “all children are made in the image of God.”

Even some blue-state Democrats have walked back their support for trans rights. Newsom, a longstanding supporter of LGBTQ rights, drew criticism last year when he told the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk that it was “deeply unfair” for trans athletes to participate in girls sports.

And the issue became a dominant theme in the recent Democratic Senate primary in Massachusetts. Sen. Edward J. Markey embraced trans rights and credited the issue for helping him defeat Rep. Seth Moulton, who told The New York Times in 2024 that he didn’t want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.” (He later apologized.)

Off-year example

The topic of transgender athletes in women’s sports may be less politically potent now than it was in 2024 — at least if elections since then are any indication. In the 2025 Virginia governor’s race, for example, Republican Winsome Earle-Sears’ campaign spent millions on ads attacking Democratic now-Gov. Abigail Spanberger on trans issues, to no avail. 

Still, Republicans in tight races are hoping it continues to have legs. In the battle for Iowa’s open Senate seat, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson ran ads this summer claiming Democrat Josh Turek supports “sex changes for kids.” Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold-winning wheelchair basketball athlete, told The New York Times in July, “As someone that spent a lot of my life in high-level sports, I don’t believe that biological males should compete against females in sports.”

Ahead of the hearing on the Hill this week, Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal said Republicans “don’t have a constructive proposal” to take home to voters, a claim echoed by Vermont Sen. Peter Welch, a fellow Democrat on the Judiciary panel.

Republicans “want to change the topic from their failure to address affordability to culture war issues,” Welch said. 

Asked about Democratic candidates moving to the center on this issue, he said, “They’re running to win.”

Now? The president has a net approval rating of -77 points.

news.title: The 2028 presidential race is already here — and it’s early
news.text:
Summer’s swampy heat released its grip on Washington Tuesday as if someone had flipped a switch.

Fall is not the only new season stirring.

The 2028 presidential race, which has long felt like a distant hypothetical amid the wrenching turmoil of President Donald Trump’s early second term, has suddenly sprung into life.

Possible Democratic and Republican contenders are hitting the midterm trail in states that just happen to hold early presidential contests. They’re wading into top policy issues. A few openly yearn for the White House. Some make cryptic comments to keep a door open. Others wonder whether they have a lane.

The sense that a clock is ticking even drew in Trump, who is loath to admit he’s only leasing power. In a UN General Assembly address Tuesday, he reminded his foes in Tehran: “I’ll be here for two and a half years.”

It’s normal for possible presidential candidates to become more visible around this time. Midterm elections offer them cover to engage base voters. They can test new stump lines, assess the political mood, lay down informal early state infrastructure and bank favors with grateful candidates.

But the 2028 campaign suddenly seems more tangible, perhaps because Trump’s fragile political state is inducing end-of-an-era vibes and Democrats have finally stopped mourning the 2024 presidential election.

That debacle was fresh on minds Tuesday when former Vice President Kamala Harris, the party’s last-minute nominee, showed up in Michigan to try to unite Democrats behind Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

She’s not the only possible 2028 Democrat making noise. New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has a progressive juggernaut rolling. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff hasn’t even won reelection, but 2028 buzz is building. Govs. JB Pritzker, Andy Beshear and Josh Shapiro are also on maneuvers.

On the GOP side, every word and gesture by Vice President JD Vance takes on extra meaning as he steels himself for the unfathomable task of a possible presidential run under Trump’s nose. And Sen. Ted Cruz, Sen. Rand Paul and other potential GOP candidates are also openly mulling a run. Even 74-year-old Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy told the Washington Post in an article published Tuesday that while he’s planning on running for reelection, he might take a tilt at the top job “if a bunch of goobers” run for president.

It’s that moment in a nascent presidential season when countless politicians look in the mirror and wonder why not them. At a testing time for US democracy, it’s reassuring that presidential spring training is near.

What each party needs in 2028

The 2028 election, with two open national party tickets, will mark a new political era.

The eventual Republican nominee will have to decide whether there’s a future for MAGA or if the party’s dormant, traditional conservative roots should be revived.

Democrats need someone to unify progressives and moderates. An anti-Trump platform may work in the midterms. But polls show an electorate still sour on a party that lost their confidence when Joe Biden was president.

The White House rumor mill slipped into higher gear Tuesday with an intriguing New York Times interview with Ocasio-Cortez. The New York Democrat’s midterm travels are positioning her as the inheritor of Bernie Sanders’ progressive movement. She’s adept at creating splashy viral moments that define Trump-era politics, like her August announcement that she was freezing her eggs.

Ocasio-Cortez, soon to turn 37, told the Times she’s wrestling with the intangible question that can define a presidential campaign. “There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she said. But after two of the last three Democratic nominees were women and both lost, Ocasio-Cortez also seemed to question her ceiling. “I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability,” she said.

Harris epitomizes such questions. She made her fall debut in one of seven swing states that she lost to Trump in 2024. She has not decided whether to run again.

But other Democrats are pre-positioning, including a number of governors. Shapiro, who seems to be cruising to reelection in Pennsylvania, last week addressed a pressing national question — whether to place guardrails on artificial intelligence — and condemned Trump’s claim that concerns about the technology’s destructive potential are a “hoax.”

Beshear on Tuesday published a new book, “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken Country” — using a classic tactic of heartland leaders who need to build a national profile. “We need to show up in places that we haven’t been in far too long. We need to show up in coal mining communities, in farming communities, and listen to the needs of people,” the Kentucky governor told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on Monday. Asked whether he’d run in 2028, he insisted: “I haven’t made any decision on that.”

Pritzker, of Illinois, has shown Democratic voters he can stick it to Trump. But he’s in the news for a more personal reason after revealing he’s shed 80 pounds on GLP-1 medication. He told CBS News he’s concentrating on his reelection bid and has “not made any decisions about what I might do in the future.”

Another Trump foe, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, said at last week’s Atlantic Festival of a possible presidential campaign: “The answer is I might, I just haven’t decided.”

Where does the GOP go after Trump?

Trump has seemed to enjoy jokingly playing off potential heirs like Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But the game will be less fun when he’s a lame duck. The veep is widely seen as a Republican front-runner, and there has been no sign from Rubio that he plans to run. Vance Friday traveled to Iowa, a GOP early state that shows the perils of a presidential campaign. Trump’s unpopularity in a reliable red bastion has left Senate and gubernatorial races surprisingly close.

The vice president’s balancing act and thin record of winning elections in his own right — he was in the Senate for only two years before his current job — explain why he’s unlikely to clear the field.

Former GOP presidential candidate Ted Cruz, who won 11 state contests as runner-up to Trump in the 2016 Republican nominating race, seems to be itching to run again. “It’s no secret that I want to be president,” Cruz said on Texas Lt. Gov Dan Patrick’s podcast in August. He’s not yet made a final decision.

Other possible GOP candidates include Texas Gov. Greg Abbott; outgoing Florida governor and defeated 2024 GOP candidate Ron DeSantis; and Florida Sen. Rick Scott.

Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, who lost to Trump in 2016, is calling for a free market, anti-tariff candidate to balance Trump-style populism. Will it be him? Paul told the Post he’s 50-50 on making the race.

But maybe there’s a lurker candidate no one has thought of. After all, Trump was regarded as a joke before his anti-establishment takeover of the GOP in 2016. And Democrats seem primed for their own populist takeover.

The name of the next president may not currently be the biggest issue — the midterm endgame and the war in Iran matter more right now.

But when America awakes on November 4, after a late night watching John King call congressional races on CNN’s Magic Wall, the next presidential election will truly begin.

And both parties will increasingly look to a future beyond Trump.

news.title: Usha Vance was ‘50 billion times better’ than JD - and joins cohort of first and second ladies to outshine future husbands in college
news.text:
Long before their husbands were elected president or vice president, several of America’s future first and second ladies had already eclipsed them in the law school classroom.

Usha Vance was described as “50 billion times better” than JD Vance in a moot court exercise, in a recent Vanity Fair profile of the vice president which spoke to their former professors and classmates at Yale. Hillary Clinton was remembered as a relentless go-getter, while Bill Clinton rarely attended class. And when a professor was asked to compare Barack and Michelle Obama, he offered an unvarnished assessment: “She was better.”

While the sample size is small, the pattern is striking.

Only four first or second ladies attended law school, long a training ground for America’s political elite. Each met her future husband there or arrived on campus ahead of him. Again and again, people who knew them at the time recalled a similar dynamic: The women were the standouts, seemingly destined to play second fiddle to no one.

The pattern raises obvious questions: Did America elect the wrong spouses? What stopped the women from running and winning?

Political scientists point to several factors, including the male-dominated nature of politics, long-standing sexism and a persistent gender gap in political ambition. Men, research has found, are more likely than women to seek office — including when women have comparable or stronger credentials.

Marilyn Quayle, the daughter of Hoosier State physicians, began taking night classes at the Indiana University School of Law in the 1970s. There, she met and married Dan Quayle, the future vice president under George H.W. Bush.

The couple sat together in tax lectures, but Marilyn Quayle drove much of the discussion and regularly sought out the professor afterward, Time reported in 1989. Classmates nicknamed her “superwoman” for balancing family responsibilities with law school. While pregnant, she even induced labor early so she could take the bar exam.

That reputation endured as her husband rose through politics.

“To be honest with you, I was campaigning for the Senate one time, and someone came up to me and said, 'I went to law school with your wife.' And I said, yeah, I was there too,” Dan Quayle later said.

In 1988, the year Bush chose Dan Quayle as his running mate, The Washington Post reported that stories about Marilyn Quayle’s classroom prowess had circulated for years.

“Over and over, men and women who attended night law school at the University of Indiana in the early '70s say flatly that Marilyn Tucker – a bright, friendly, industrious young woman determinedly bound for a career – was smarter than her good-looking, somewhat lackadaisical classmate, Dan Quayle,” the outlet reported.

Hillary Clinton attended law school at roughly the same time, studying at Yale Law School in Connecticut from 1969 to 1973.

There, she met her future husband, Bill Clinton. The pair first spoke in the library after Hillary Rodham, as she was then known, approached him and said: “If you're going to keep staring at me, and now I'm staring back, we at least ought to know each other's name.”

Years later, several classmates remembered Hillary Clinton, a Wellesley graduate, as the stronger student out of the couple.

“Hillary was the first to raise her hand and almost always had the correct answer,” former Labor Secretary Robert Reich recalled. “I raised my hand fairly often but got it wrong half the time. Bill missed most classes.”

“When we were in law school, she was by far a better student than either Bill Clinton or me,” Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal told a local news outlet in 2015.

The trend continued with Michelle Obama, who graduated from Harvard Law School in 1988 — the same year her future husband began classes there. The two later met at Sidley & Austin in Chicago, where the future first lady, then Michelle Robinson, was assigned to mentor Barack Obama.

When asked to compare the two, their former Harvard Law School professor Charles Ogletree offered a blunt assessment.

“[Obama’s] wife should have been president,” he told TMZ in 2017. “He was great, too, but she was better…She could easily be president, but I don’t think she will.”

Usha Vance, the California-born daughter of Indian immigrants, was no exception. Like Hillary Clinton, she met her future husband at Yale Law School — and, according to those who knew them, outshone him there.

She was “pegged as the brightest student in the class of 2013, possibly even a future president,” Vanity Fair reported earlier this month.

One classmate called her a “rock star.” And a former professor recalled her dramatically outperforming JD Vance during a moot court exercise, telling the outlet: “I gotta tell you, Usha must have been 50 billion times better than [Vance] was at that assignment.”

The experiences of these four highly accomplished law students — all of whom went on to help elect their husbands — raise pointed questions about gender and political power. For one, why didn’t academic success translate into electoral victories?

Michele Swers, a professor of American government at Georgetown University, said that talents that prove useful in the classroom may not necessarily lend themselves to campaigning for and holding office.

“Bill Clinton had certain political skills that translated in communication,” Swers told The Independent. “Law school is trying to teach you to be very detail-oriented and, you know, write successful briefs, which are not always the skills of politics.”

Kathleen Dolan, a professor emerita of political science at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, pointed to a broader obstacle: the longstanding dominance of men in positions of political power.

“I mean, men are much more likely to be elected leaders in our country,” Dolan told The Independent. “They have always been more likely to be elected leaders.”

The United States, unlike 63 other nations, has never had a female head of government and only elected its first female vice president in 2020. Women, who secured the right to vote nationwide in 1920, hold only about 28 percent of seats in the current Congress.

Dolan, whose research focuses on women and politics, said the four women also reflect an enduring “gender gap in political ambition.”

“Men are much, much more likely to run for office than are women. news.text: A Team Trump social media account has ignited fierce online controversy by utilising promotional imagery and music from Taylor Swift's newly announced single 'Patient Zero' in a political immigration post.The post paired the artwork with Swift's song 'Father Figure' and a claim about border crossings, drawing criticism from some users online.Published on 23 September 2026, the Team Trump post used a mock CD cover carrying the phrase, 'And, baby, that's sh0w business for y0u.' Public reporting did not establish that Swift personally ordered every removal.That earlier history gives the latest post more context, but it does not establish why Swift's artwork or music was selected. No evidence reviewed for this article shows that President Donald Trump personally directed the 23 September post.The distinction matters because the criticism on X often referred to Trump himself. Reuters reported the message after Swift endorsed Harris, who was then Trump's Democratic opponent in the 2024 presidential election.That history helps explain why another Swift-themed political post attracted attention online. It does not prove fixation, obsession or an attempt to provoke the singer, despite those interpretations appearing in some social-media reactions.The immigration claim remains the clearest factual issue in the latest post. Official records show thousands of Southwest Border Patrol apprehensions in 2025, while the administration's documented zero figure concerns releases into the United States.As the entertainment industry and political strategists monitor future developments, the viral post serves as another reminder of how deeply pop culture and partisan politics intertwine in modern digital campaigning.

news.title: Judge dismisses newspaper lawsuit in another blow to Trump
news.text:
An Iowa district court judge on Wednesday dismissed the lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump against the Des Moines Register and pollster J. Ann Selzer for the 2024 Iowa Poll published shortly before the election.

Trump filed the lawsuit against the Iowa newspaper; its parent company, Gannett Co., now renamed USA Today Co.; Selzer and her polling company in 2024 after winning the U.S. presidential race against former Vice President Kamala Harris. An Iowa Poll published three days before the 2024 election showed Harris leading Trump among likely Iowa voters 47% to 44%. Trump won Iowa in the 2024 presidential election by 13 percentage points.

The lawsuit alleges the poll was an attempt to “create a false narrative of inevitability for Harris in the final week of the 2024 Presidential Election.”

The lawsuit went from federal court to state court in 2025, when Trump’s attorneys refiled the lawsuit alongside U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former state Sen. Brad Zaun. While Trump’s attorneys had claimed the poll results were “brazen election interference” and a violation of Iowa’s Consumer Fraud Act, District Court Judge Scott Beattie said the claim was incorrect.

Beattie wrote in his ruling, “at its core, the plaintiffs’ petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability.”

The judge dismissed the case with prejudice, meaning Trump will not be able to file the same legal claim.

The organization representing Selzer, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), released a statement celebrating the decision Wednesday.

“We’re pleased that the court recognized what we’ve said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought,” FIRE Chief Counsel Bob Corn-Revere said in a statement. “The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of ‘fake news.’ That may work for him as a campaign slogan, but it is not a thing in the law.”

Selzer reiterated in a statement that the difference between polling and election results are not a deliberate act, nor evidence of fraud.

“Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome,” Selzer said. “What we can guarantee is that we will follow the data wherever it leads, even when the results are uncomfortable or unexpected. I am grateful that Judge Beattie’s ruling recognizes these principles and reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference.”

Attorney Alan Ostergren, who represented the president in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the case dismissal.

news.title: Maine voters see Susan Collins as an institution. They haven’t formed much of a view about her Democratic foe.
news.text:
For the first installment of MS NOW’s “The Voter Files,” we brought together two groups of Maine voters in the Lewiston and Auburn area who have supported federal candidates from both parties to discuss how they are planning to vote in the 2026 Senate race, or why they are still undecided.

For the first group, we heard from 10 working-class voters from Maine’s 2nd Congressional District who identified themselves as moderates or who said they lean Republican but sometimes defect. Five had voted for Donald Trump and three for Kamala Harris in 2024, while nine voted for Maine Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who represents one of the most conservative House districts in the country.

The discussion took place on Sept. 15, and the group was composed of registered voters who told us they planned to vote in November in the congressional elections.

For the second group, we heard from 10 women in the Lewiston and Auburn area who identified as independents and voted for Republican Sen. Susan Collins in previous elections. Seven of these women voted for Harris in 2024. Collins is running in a tough re-election contest against Democrat Troy Jackson that is key to whether Republicans can maintain Senate control after November..

The discussions were designed to mirror focus groups conducted by a campaign. We hired a nonpartisan outside firm to help gather the right voters, and I led the wide-ranging conversations covering personal experiences, political leanings and impressions of candidates that influenced the participants’ decision-making in the Senate race.

Alongside polling, the findings illuminate the tensions, information and reasoning process driving these likely voters as they head to the ballot box in just a few weeks. Although Auburn has been a bellwether in the past two presidential cycles — closely tracking Maine’s presidential and Collins’ 2020 Senate margins by within three-tenths of a point — these findings are neither representative of the broader Maine electorate nor predictive of the upcoming Senate election’s outcome.

Perhaps unique to Maine, Susan Collins was viewed by those we spoke to as an independent Maine institution. Her 30 years in office and reputation for constituent services offset Trump’s national unpopularity, according to what we heard.

MS NOW’s elections team currently rates the Maine Senate race as a toss-up, and some of the latest polling has Collins and Jackson essentially deadlocked. But the 2020 Maine Senate race is a humbling reminder that polling alone often can't predict an outcome. Collins consistently trailed Democrat Sara Gideon, in some polls by double digits, before winning by almost 9 percentage points on election day.

Maine is one of the last holdouts of split-ticket voters who may lean Democratic at the top of the ticket yet still view Collins as an institutional necessity. These voters don't always behave the way the numbers suggest.

Here’s what we found was on their minds.

The cost-of-living spike has fundamentally changed the way Americans live

No casual trips to town. No vacations or Christmas gifts for relatives. Cutting wood for heat and second jobs. The grim economic outlook of the Maine voters we spoke to is the lens through which they evaluate their electoral choices. The rising cost of living has changed how the people we talked to live day to day, but they see business as usual in their politicians. Winter is coming, in the most literal sense, for Mainers facing a 74% spike in the cost of heating oil and trying to figure out how to survive the season.

A Maine institution: Collins

Perhaps unique to Maine, Collins was viewed by those we spoke to as an independent Maine institution. Her 30 years in office and reputation for constituent services offset Trump’s national unpopularity, according to what we heard. One voter said, “The lady shows up for work,” a notable act in an era of chaos. 

Other voters cited Collins’ perceived deliverables as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee: defense spending for local shipyards, resources for rural hospitals and Social Security funds for Maine teachers. The focus groups were conducted before the publication of the ProPublica story on the Trump administration’s FBI shutting down its probe into alleged illegal donations to Collins’ 2020 campaign committee.

Unknown and undefined: Jackson

Since becoming the nominee in July, after Graham Platner dropped out, Jackson has struggled to define himself as a viable replacement for Collins. I found that Jackson has an increasingly shrinking window — a few weeks, and the clock is ticking — to define himself amid the GOP barrage of negative ads from outside groups. (The New York Times estimates that $27.1 million in pro-Democratic and $47.4 million in pro-Republican anonymous ad spending breaks down to about $80 for each of the fewer than 900,000 registered voters in Maine.)

So far, Jackson’s campaign has focused on attacking Collins and emphasizing his working-class background, while offering few concrete policy ideas or proposals. The voters we heard from want to hear a vision and a plan to make their lives better, and the vision vacuum they see extends to the national Democratic Party.

Even our participants in the second group, most of whom voted for Harris, struggled to name what Democrats stood for in 2026. In the aftermath of Platner’s rise and fall, what they saw as incompetence on a state level extended to the Democrats more broadly. In other words, no affirmative vision makes these voters hesitate to leave Collins.

If I were advising Jackson

As a relative unknown, Jackson needs to prove that he can go to the Senate and deliver as effectively as Collins. Instead of concentrating on ads tying her to Trump, Jackson has to get voters to question what they are getting from Collins’ perceived Washington clout on healthcare, the economy and heating costs. He needs to turn the incumbent's greatest strength — her seniority — into a liability, by tying her five terms to what they see as the status quo.

The Democratic base cares about Trump. But Trump is not a defining factor for the ticket splitters deciding between the comfort of Collins' seniority versus Jackson’s inexperience in Washington. His background as a logger will not win this election, but demonstrating to voters that he has a plan for healthcare and heating assistance once in Washington might.

If I were advising Collins

Incumbency and seniority may well propel Collins into her sixth term, but she needs to reassure the independent women who feel betrayed by her critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who joined the 5-4 vote to overturn Roe v. Wade. According to the voters we spoke to, a sincere acknowledgement that she misjudged Kavanaugh’s reassurances that Roe was settled precedent might help win them back. For more on how these voters view Collins and the overturning of Roe, watch “The Voter Files.”

Methodology

We used an independent firm to recruit likely voters, who were paid an industry-standard fee for their participation. Over 90 minutes on Sept. 15, our questions explored participants' specific life experiences, turning points and trade-offs between someone they know and someone they don’t.

news.title: 'Very scary': Diehard Republicans flirt with the unthinkable in Trump country
news.text:
GRAPEVINE — Jill Tate has spent 30 years building and maintaining the Republican majority in Texas.

In all that time, she’s never been more worried about an election.

“This is truly the first time I’ve felt in my bones we could lose the Texas House, and we could lose a statewide seat,” Tate said. “And that’s very scary.”

Now president of Texas Federation of Republican Women, Tate organizes over 10,000 women who do the hard work behind the party’s dominant grassroots operation — calling and texting voters, block walking, producing voter guides and sending postcards.

If her fears come to pass, it could be Tate’s backyard — the fast-growing, diverse suburbs of the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex — that delivers Texas to the Democrats. 

Long associated with the country club types who formed a backbone of red Texas, the area is in the midst of enormous change driven by rapid population growth, corporate relocations and shifting political views in the Trump era. 

The change makes suburban voters — and suburban women in particular — a key swing bloc that U.S. Senate candidates Ken Paxton and James Talarico are chasing this November.

But with the election less than six weeks away, Republicans worry the region’s typically reliable voters, disenchanted by Paxton’s political baggage, could sit out the Senate race, a hesitancy that also could endanger GOP candidates for the Legislature, county commission and justices of the peace. 

In interviews with over a dozen people in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, many Republicans said they were struggling with how to vote in the Senate contest or knew friends and neighbors who were. 

Jayne Howell, who chaired the Denton County GOP from 2018 to 2022, said that six months ago, she was leaning toward not voting in the Senate race. Now, she’s decided to vote for Paxton — but she knows not everyone has had the same evolution.

“I felt like he was going to vote for more conservative policies than his opponent,” Howell said at a coffee shop in Lewisville, a suburb about 25 miles north of Dallas. “So I’m going to vote for Paxton. It goes against my personal beliefs, but I don’t want Talarico to win. But I think there’s a lot of people that aren’t going to even come out to vote. That’s going to affect the down-ballot races.”

Some, describing their hesitation or opposition as faith-based, cited accusations of extramarital affairs by Paxton. His wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton, cited adultery in her 2025 divorce petition.

Some voters lumped Paxton in with a GOP they have soured on during President Donald Trump’s second term. Others were turned off by allegations of corruption stemming from a 2015 indictment for felony securities fraud (charges were dropped in 2024 after Paxton, who didn’t admit guilt, agreed to 100 hours of community service, 15 hours of ethics training and $271,000 in restitution) and 2023 articles of impeachment accusing him of misusing his office to benefit a friend and political donor (the Texas Senate voted to acquit him after a two-week trial). 

Dan Pence, a 68-year-old in Rowlett, has voted Republican in nearly every election in his life. After voting for Trump in 2024, he’s found himself frustrated with the direction of the party. He still believes he will stick with Republicans for most statewide races, but he’s undecided in the Senate contest — and leaning toward Talarico, whom he thinks he could “hold my nose” and vote for. Paxton, he said, is a bridge too far.

“I can’t verbalize how much I dislike that guy,” Pence said. “I wouldn’t even want to be in the same room as him. He exudes slimy.”

In the 2024 presidential election, nearly one in four Texas votes came from the region’s core four counties — Dallas, Tarrant, Collin and Denton — making them enormously important to both candidates’ hopes for success. The suburban area was a Republican stronghold before 2016 but has trended more blue in recent election cycles.

Democrats flipped Tarrant County in the 2018 U.S. Senate race and narrowly won the county in the 2024 Senate race even as the state lurched right. Collin County, home to Plano and Frisco, has remained narrowly red despite statewide shifts, with Beto O’Rourke, Joe Biden and Colin Allred receiving 46% to 47% of the vote despite running in wildly different cycles. Even Denton County, traditionally the most Republican of the bunch, has seen slippage in GOP support after Trump won by 20 points in 2016 and 13.1 points in 2024. 

To succeed in these counties, the Republican turnout operation will need to convert the hesitant. 

The Texas Federation of Republican Women this fall will host weekends of mass action in Tarrant, Williamson and Collin counties — all with significant suburban populations — to promote state-level and down-ballot Republican candidates and encourage voters to support the entire ticket. 

In addition, numerous GOP candidates and organizers said they are emphasizing to friends and neighbors the old adage that a vote is a chess move rather than a valentine.

“I have tried to say to some of our ladies who are not especially enthusiastic about voting for [Paxton] — and it’s not just him, there’s some other candidates [who are] not their favorite — we may not have perfect candidates, because we’re all human,” Tate said. “We all make mistakes. But we have perfect ideals.”

Kronda Thimesch, a former Republican state representative from Denton County who voted to impeach Paxton and then lost a GOP primary, is president of her local Republican women’s club. She said friends from church with deeply held biblical values are struggling with how to vote this November, and in some cases are so put off by Paxton that they’re planning to skip the election entirely.

“There are a lot of people that I’ve been having conversations with, [telling them] if you can’t vote for one Republican, please continue to go down ballot and vote for the rest,” said Thimesch, who lost her 2024 primary to Paxton impeachment attorney Mitch Little. “But unfortunately, a lot of people, they don’t even want to walk into the polling location and vote — which is disheartening.”

Despite hesitation from some voters, Paxton can still expect to get hundreds of thousands of votes out of these counties. Trump, as Paxton has noted, has been dogged by some of the same ethical baggage yet won Tarrant, Collin and Denton counties in 2024 en route to a blowout in the state. 

His campaign believes it has a compelling story to tell suburban women. One pro-Paxton ad focuses on a sex trafficking case that his office prosecuted. And the campaign plans to emphasize the attorney general’s record pursuing consumer protection lawsuits on issues suburban women care about.

“Suburban moms want someone who will actually fight the people putting their kids in harm’s way: Big Food, Big Pharma, and Big Tech,” Paxton spokesperson Madison Cercy said in a statement, citing the attorney general’s lawsuits targeting misleading food labeling, forever chemicals and social media platforms that create addiction among kids. 

“They’re not looking for someone who treats their kids upbringing as a social experiment and views public safety as optional,” Cercy said. “Ken Paxton is the fighter they have already trusted and the one they need, and that is the message our campaign will be bringing to them.”

Polling suggests Paxton still has work to do to consolidate the Republican base — work that the various groups making up the Republican ground game are undertaking as get-out-the-vote efforts ramp up. Down-ballot candidates also are working their territories across the region, well aware of the stakes the Senate race could pose.

Shelby Williams, a former Collin County GOP chair now running for county commission in a purple district in the west of the county, said he leads with local policy — infrastructure, property taxes, water — rather than his partisan allegiance. He has heard people “here and there” say they’re planning to skip the Senate race. Like Tate, he wants voters to see that the election is a binary choice and encourages them to look at both candidates’ records. 

“Especially amongst the Christian right — and I am a devout Christian — there’s a tendency to look at the stains and say, well I can’t get behind so-and-so,” Williams said. “Well, OK, you have to inspect the alternative — even if the alternative is an undervote. You’re going to vote for something, even if it’s by your inaction.”

The Paxton campaign is emphasizing the dangers of an undervote as well.

“The stakes are clear: if voters stay home in the suburbs, they are not sitting out a personality contest. They are leaving their kids’ food, phones, schools, and streets to the politician who has proven he will not fight those fights,” Cercy said.

Ross Hunt, a GOP operative in Dallas, said the Republican base rapidly consolidated behind Paxton after he secured the nomination in May, but the pace and intensity has not been uniform across regions. 

Hunt said he is more concerned about Republicans skipping the Senate race in North Texas than in other parts of the state.

“Consolidation has been stronger — not universally — but it’s been stronger in other areas of the state than it has been in D-FW,” Hunt said. “And some of that has to do with the fact that we just have more George Bush-style Republicans up here. That’s part of it. Some of it I think has to do with the fact that we have a lot of voters up here who are economically motivated, and are not really culture warriors at all, and are looking for someone who’s focused on those issues.”

What’s troubling the suburbs

Laura Hill, the Republican mayor of Southlake from 2015 to 2021, hasn’t missed an election since Gerald Ford was president.

Hill runs in a wide circle of women in the Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs — women she described as successful, well-educated and politically engaged. But this cycle, many of them have told her they’re planning to skip the Senate race on their ballots. Hill intends to do the same — and feels like the GOP political culture in Tarrant County has left her feeling increasingly unwelcome, particularly after losing a 2022 Texas House primary that she said included personal attacks on her businesses, employees and parents.

“I think we’ve created monsters — and that’s what my friends are saying,” Hill said. “We’ve all done things that we’ve had to ask for forgiveness, and that is between us and our Lord. But at some point, you no longer speak for the Lord when you continue to have to ask for forgiveness and you have a chosen lifestyle. Live it! But don’t tell me that I need to vote for you just because you are a Republican.”

Hill said among the skeptical Republican women she’s talked to, about 40 percent plan to vote for Talarico.

Dorothy Burton, the former Republican mayor pro tem of Duncanville, left the GOP in 2019 and now considers herself partyless. A member of Republicans for Talarico, Burton believes there’s a quiet network of Republicans planning to pull the lever for the Democrat while continuing to vote with the GOP in other races. 

Being a Republican, she said, is about more than a party — it’s an identity. But she believes the willingness by some in the GOP to criticize Paxton will let more Bush-aligned Republicans vote for Talarico — or skip the race — without feeling like they’re compromising that identity.

“Now that some have given permission that it is OK to vote for Talarico, it’s like, I can do that and still be Republican,” Burton said. 

John Huffman, a Republican who followed Hill as Southlake mayor and finished third in the initial special election for Senate District 9 in the Fort Worth area, has been a vocal critic of his party’s direction and the political doom he believes it could bring in November.

“I especially think suburban women — but maybe just your average suburban professional in Tarrant County and elsewhere — looks at Paxton, and looks at the personal and the professional and political baggage he comes with, and starts to think: is this the best we have?” Huffman said. “Is this really the best we can do as Republicans?”

A good portion of the more establishment wing of the party will likely come home for Paxton. Republican advertising has gone hard on Talarico, criticizing his record on taxes and comments supporting transgender Texans, to drive home the point that a Talarico victory would be anathema to their values.

Darlene Stanaland, a 79-year-old in Frisco, voted for Paxton in the primary and plans to vote for him again in the general election. 

Stanaland first met Paxton, a longtime fixture in Collin County politics, years ago at a Tea Party protest outside Frisco City Hall. She appreciated that Paxton was active in filing legal challenges against the Biden administration.

“He at least fights for Texas,” Stanaland said. “That’s more than most of them do.”

Stanaland, a lifelong Republican who never misses an election, said her social circle is also firmly behind Paxton.

“Everybody’s got a past and everybody’s got a personal life, and that’s not what this is about,” she said. “This is about conserving our state, and I think he does that.”

But Huffman, who said he cannot vote for Paxton and likely will skip the Senate race, believes the Republican Party will leave votes on the table — support it potentially cannot afford to lose. 

“As a candidate, you're trying to sell yourself — and you sell on trust,” Huffman said. “And there are so many issues with Paxton. He has broken trust with many, many people. I think for him particularly, you are testing the outer limits of the average general election voter's ability to be loyal to the concept of lesser of two evils.”

Several lifelong Republican voters from the Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs echoed Huffman’s sentiment. 

Kelly Sayre, a 75-year-old in Corinth, was once the Denton County GOP vice chair. But he became disillusioned with the GOP after the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol; in 2024, he voted for Kamala Harris for president and Ted Cruz for Senate.

Sayre said he thinks he’ll vote for Talarico this November — both as an opportunity to vote against Trump and Paxton (“I just don’t believe he’s a good person”) and because he sees something positive in the Democratic seminarian.

“After 10 or 12 years of name-calling and outright cruelty, I don’t see that coming from him,” Sayre said. “People feel differently about this, but for me, it’s important in that I see him to be a practicing Christian that’s far closer to living like we’re supposed to live than the alternative.” 

Betty Graham, an 82-year-old in Plano, is a lifelong Republican who voted for Trump two years ago. A native of West Texas, she recalled meeting George H.W. Bush at a fundraiser in Abilene in the 1980s and working on a Republican campaign in Nolan County. But she’s been disappointed by the president’s second term — especially over the Iran war and the administration’s pursuit of border infrastructure in Big Bend National Park and surrounding areas. 

Graham has come to regret her Trump vote and finds herself heartbroken by the direction of the party. She could have voted for Cornyn, she said, but refuses to vote for Paxton. Now, she considers herself an independent — and she’s planning to skip the race or vote Libertarian. Voting for a Democrat is out of the question.

“I can’t, in good conscience, vote on any of the Republicans,” Graham said. “And I certainly am not going to vote on the Democrat, because I don’t believe their ideology at all.”

Democrats see an opportunity

Voters like Graham represent the potential and the pitfalls for Talarico. 

Every Republican voter who skips the contest helps the Democrat, but to win, Talarico also needs to pick up crossover and independent support. Republicans are now spending tens of millions to emphasize Talarico’s negatives in the hope of moving unsure or unmotivated Republicans into Paxton’s camp.

This is not the first statewide race where Democrats have looked to the suburbs for an edge — and in the past, they’ve ultimately been disappointed. In 2018, O’Rourke posted the best results Democrats had seen in decades in Tarrant, Collin and Denton counties but still lost to Cruz by 2.6 percentage points. In 2020, Biden saw record high Democratic vote totals and similar percentages to O’Rourke but lost the state by 5 points. And even as Allred achieved similar results in Tarrant, Collin and Denton counties as his Democratic predecessors, he lost to Cruz by a larger margin in 2024 as his party underperformed in the urban cores and in South Texas.

The results beg the question: Are there enough untapped suburban votes for Talarico and Democrats to capitalize on?

State Sen. Taylor Rehmet, a Garland mechanic and union leader, represents the bullish case for Democrats. In a district Trump won by 17 points in 2024, Rehmet emerged from a January special election with a 14-point victory in a Tarrant County district that contains a portion of Fort Worth and its northern suburbs. Special elections, with smaller totals, can produce unusual results — but Rehmet’s victory in Senate District 9 inspired enormous Democratic enthusiasm.

Democrats see opportunity beyond dissatisfied Republicans — enthusiasm driving increased turnout by their voters and swings away from the GOP in the suburban Hispanic population. Rehmet relied on both in his shocking special election victory in Tarrant County.

“People are targeting the working class folks,” said Allison Campolo, chair of the Tarrant County Democratic Party. “We are a county with a huge amount of working class people, but also a lot of union people — Lockheed Martin, Bell Helicopter, a bunch of others. And so making sure that these working-class union voters know who's standing up for workers' rights, affordability and good jobs is a really big deal.”

Majority-Hispanic precincts shifted by an average of 34 percentage points toward Rehmet relative to the 2022 race for the Senate district. Jason Villalba, a former Republican state representative from Dallas who runs the Texas Hispanic Policy Foundation, said even with the usual caveats about low turnout in special elections, the size of the Hispanic vote swing toward Rehmet was too large to be dismissed. 

He suspects the swing is not limited to Fort Worth.

“You’re seeing similar effects, at least anecdotally, in all of the major suburbs,” Villalba said. “Plano is largely Hispanic … we’re seeing the same trends. Arlington, Grand Prairie, Cedar Hill, Mansfield — all of it showing the same trends.”

Democrats also believe a bevy of newer issues — frustration with data centers and Flock cameras among them — will drive voters toward the party. Numerous Democrats also said the state’s ban on several hemp-derived THC products is an issue they’re hearing a surprising amount about as they campaign door to door.

Delia Parker-Mims, chair of the Denton County Democratic Party, said THC could be a sleeper issue for suburban women and younger voters. There are smoke shops, she said, in the more middle class and well-to-do suburbs, and middle-age women are increasingly using THC products for health reasons. 

“[Housewives] are into THC, and now you’re taking that away,” Parker-Mims said. “I do think that is pissing a lot of people off.”

Some Republicans agree that this cycle is different from past ones. Many emphasized that in 2018, when Republicans narrowly held onto victory, Cruz had the Republican Party unified behind him.

But in the Metroplex, some no longer see that enthusiasm. Several GOP voters who plan to leave the Senate race blank or vote for Talarico also stressed they would’ve had no trouble voting for Cornyn.

Hill consistently voted for Cornyn and Cruz, saying they “carry themselves in a manner that is important to our party.”

“I think because we have so much power and we think Republicans are untouchable in Texas, we’ve decided that we can put up anybody,” she said.

This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

news.title: Andy Burnham’s Ministry of Truth
news.text:
With an increasingly paranoid tone, the report describes how internal ‘extremists [who] are exploiting people’s fears for their own purpose’ work in concert with ‘malign foreign influence’, in ‘online echo chambers’ where harm is ‘exacerbated by malevolent algorithms’. The last claim is particularly bizarre. For the British state in 2026 has become so paranoid that it believes algorithms have moral agency and are out to get it.

It is then, no wonder that the state is seeking to establish greater control over speech which it feels threatens it. Of course, simultaneously, the state is lying more and more. It is fighting a court battle to avoid publishing data it holds on migrant crime rates. It has spent the last year claiming that the early release scheme is perfectly safe because those set free will be tightly managed via tagging, only for it to emerge this week that they won’t be tagged because there’s no capacity. And this week, the boats bringing illegal migrants ashore turned off their transponders to disguise where they planned to land. The state lies all the time, and it projects that dishonesty onto those who challenge its goals. So of course it intends to establish a ‘National Centre’ to oversee speech. Of course we must have a Ministry of Truth.

Commenting on the establishment of NCID, Toby Young, Director of the Free Speech Union, told me that:

 ‘Andy Burnham sold it as a way to counter Russia’s information warfare, then, in the next breath, said it would be used to tackle threats to “community cohesion”, so there can be little doubt its main purpose will be to monitor and silence domestic dissent. It’s the latest addition to the state’s growing surveillance and suppression apparatus. Emily Thornberry welcomed this new Orwellian unit as “long overdue”, but there are at least nine others by my count. The British state is managing the indigenous population as if it was a colonial power occupying a foreign country. Got to keep a close eye on the natives and nip any potential uprisings in the bud’.

Everything Toby says is true. And there are other reasons to be concerned. The PM’s speech mentioned ‘far right’ content, but nothing about the threats from far-left agitators such as Extinction Rebellion, or Islamists, which were described as threatening our national security last week by former head of MI6, Sir Richard Dearlove. It seems that for this Prime Minister, only right-wing ideas are a threat. Similarly, it is not clear whether American content will be suppressed by the NCID. After all, the Lib Dems have called America a hostile foreign influence.

I understand that the while the British government stands by the PM’s position that we are the US’s closest ally, it is also committed to disrupting so-called foreign-state interference from any actor including the USA.

This has caused concern in Washington, including over what ‘interference’ actually means, particularly in the context of British NGOs influencing American policy on internet anonymity, both directly and via American proxies with significant foreign management. It was also noted in Washington that Labour party officials volunteered for Kamala Harris’s 2024 Presidential campaign. Given all of this, there is concern as to how NCID will behave. Indeed, a US official told me that ‘Five Eyes should mean they categorically exclude targeting us with Natsec capabilities’.

Also of concern, both in Britain and Washington, is the question of what powers this Ministry of Truth will have. How secret will its operations be? Will it be able to spy on British citizens? Will it seek to suppress and influence domestic discussion about controversial matters such as migrant crime and crumbling infrastructure? After all, as the PM said, ‘we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain.’

 It is all deeply redolent of the late Soviet Union. We must keep affirming that Britain is a multicultural success story, our health service the envy of the world, else we are doing the bidding of hostile foreign powers. And if we say the wrong thing, if we dare affirm the English ethnicity, then the Ministry of Truth will come for us.
