news.title: How Latinos became America’s biggest swing vote
news.text:
Welcome to The Midterms, Actually. Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground. Let’s get into it. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every week. Let’s get into it.
One big idea: Latinos didn’t come home. They’re just in motion.
In the last presidential election, President Donald Trump’s strong support with Latino voters ended up one of the biggest stories of the night. After years of Democrats telling themselves that the growing number of Hispanic Americans would help lead to a permanent liberal majority, their dreams were first dashed in 2016 (when many of those voters stayed home) and then buried in 2024 (when they, and other nonwhite voters, swung toward Trump).
But just as Democrats have at times been too confident that minority voters would fall in line, it now seems Republicans have replicated their mistake. Poll after poll shows a historic reversal among Latino voters in Trump’s second term, and these days even Republican members of Congress are beginning to call Trump out on his deportation efforts. 
Why? It comes back to the numbers.
As Nate Cohn observed in the New York Times this week, Democrats now lead Republicans among Hispanic likely voters by 35 percentage points on the generic congressional ballot, 64-29 — a 28-point swing from 2024, when Kamala Harris carried Hispanic voters by just 7 points. The shift is a big reason the polling has Democrats in “blue wave” territory this November.
Last week on America, Actually I explored this shift in detail — by talking to Stephanie Valencia, co-founder and president of Equis, the research firm that has spent a decade digging into the Latino electorate. And the first thing she wanted us all to know: Get rid of the idea that Latinos will ever be permanently Democratic or permanently Republican. Part of the electoral power is that a larger section of the electorate defines itself more independently.
> “Latinos often get given the title, the sleeping giant, which I just want to rid that out of everybody’s vocabulary. We should be called the swinging giant based on how much shift we have seen election to election. A third of Latinos consider themselves kind of independent or apolitical nonpartisan, and that’s that swinging middle that really is deciding every single election.”
Here are three more trends Valencia pointed out, which help explain why this all-important voting group has done such a drastic 180 on Trump in his second term.
1. It’s the economy (again)
As with all things in Trump’s second term, it starts with the fundamental problem of his second term: He has not delivered on lower prices. Equis found that Trump’s net approval with Latinos on cost of living sits at -52 — and his number on the economy (-45) is worse than his overall approval with the group (-31). Both are dramatically worse than where he sits with non-Latinos, who put him at -39 on cost of living and -25 on the economy. Among Latino men 18 to 39, cost of living hits a stunning -63.
Here’s what Valencia said:
> “Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other racial subgroup. And so what that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more. We have less savings. We have less rates of home ownership. So the kind of safety nets that other people might have, we just don’t have.”
She also pointed this out:
> “In Trump 1.0, his approval on the economy and the cost of living was actually better than his everyday approval… And he has been underwater with Latinos almost this entire term so far on the cost of living and the economy. It’s almost been a complete and total reversal.”
One of the arguments Trump made to Hispanic communities (and other groups also) was that he’d economically empower them, and that this was more important than prioritizing social causes that didn’t have a material benefit. That’s also been his fundamental flaw. From tariffs to rising gas prices, he has not only not delivered — people also feel worse off than before.
2. The immigration backlash
Valencia’s data was undeniable: More and more Latinos turned on Trump as he broadened his deportation efforts, which were broadly unpopular. But what I didn’t understand is why it took until Trump’s second term for people to realize those threats were legitimate, considering they were so front and center during his campaign. (They held up “Mass Deportation Now!” signs at the Republican National Convention!)
Here’s what Valencia said:
> “I think this is really important for us as avid news consumers to understand what it is that the average voter, and especially that voter who’s coming in and out of elections, the kind of news they’re consuming. What they were seeing on mainstream media, perhaps even Fox News at the time, was a focus on Trump surrogates who said he’s gonna focus on serious criminals, securing the border, and violent criminals. And so that’s what people bought.”
> “Fast-forward to 2026, the people who feel most regretful who voted for Trump in 2024 are most regretful because of immigration. They feel like there was a broken promise there. Like, they were told he was gonna focus on the border, which everybody agreed was chaos, and he was gonna focus on violent criminals and serious threats, and at the end of the day, he has not complied with that.”
There’s also an element of disbelief. When Trump said he would deport “bad people,” a lot of people thought he was only talking about people in other communities — or immigrants with criminal legal histories — not the more far-reaching immigration sweeps we’ve seen since he’s been in office. A striking ad from Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-FL) this week where she directly criticizes Trump’s immigration policy explicitly made this distinction. 
The Equis numbers track that shift almost perfectly. In December 2024, 65 percent of Latino Trump voters believed he would target only criminals and recent arrivals. Today, 62 percent of Latinos overall say he’s going after undocumented immigrants broadly — and among his own Latino voters, the share who say that has jumped from 26 percent to 37 percent. That perception is the whole ballgame: Latino Trump voters who still believe he’s targeting only criminals give him +84 net approval. Among those who’ve concluded he’s targeting everyone, it collapses to +31.
The backlash isn’t about the border. It’s about what’s happening in the interior — the raids, the family separations, the citizens and legal residents swept up. 
Equis finds 68 percent of Latinos say Republicans promised to deport criminals and deported hardworking people instead — and 67 percent say Democrats promise immigration reform and never deliver. Forty-two percent say both parties broke their promises.
> “I think it is a huge mistake for Democrats to assume or to rest on their laurels and think that because of what people are feeling around Trump and Republicans and the sense of disappointment and broken promises, that that is automatically going to translate to them as a party and as a brand. Right now, the Democratic brand has suffered a repeated set of blows among Latino voters. 20 years of comprehensive immigration reform that hasn’t been delivered. It’s a thing that comes up in almost every focus group.”
3. Meeting voters where they are
The third trend isn’t about persuasion at all. It’s about the fact that a lot of campaigns are still bad at the mechanics of reaching this electorate — and Valencia’s examples were almost comically basic.
Their testing found that more than 70 percent of Latinos who see an ad in Spanish come away thinking that candidate or party cares more about Latinos. That’s not a persuasion effect. That’s a respect effect, and it’s enormous for the price of one ad buy.
So how do campaigns blow it? Some examples, according to Valencia: translating English ads directly into Spanish, rather than tailoring them to the language and culture; and assuming English speakers and Spanish speakers are separate categories when voters often shift between media in both languages. 
The deeper error is the monolith problem — the group is still treated as a voting bloc that moves in unison, rather than a diverse set of people from varying countries of origin and contexts. And the fastest-moving division isn’t the country of origin at all. It’s age — an electorate replenishing itself faster than either party’s model of it.
> “There are a million Latinos who turn 18 every single year, and an 18-year-old who turns 18 this year and will vote in this year’s election was born the year Barack Obama was elected president. … The era of politics for an 18-year-old today is chaos, Covid, and corruption. They do not remember the hopium of Obama and the beautiful coalition that we built. That is all ancient history to them.”
A million new voters a year, completely up for grabs. Nobody is inheriting these voters. Neither party owns them. Because as Valencia put it: Demographics have proven not to be destiny — effort and intention matter more.
What I’m hearing
This week I called Matthew Eadie, a reporter at Evanston Now, who has been covering an ICE stop in Evanston, Illinois that has since attracted national attention. On the morning of Sunday, September 20, federal agents stopped a man walking on Howard Street. He turned out to be a US citizen, and not the person they were looking for. Agents reportedly left him on the ground with injuries to his head, neck, and teeth. DHS says he “refused to identify himself. Now the community is demanding answers.”
What’s the community reaction been?
People are really furious. If you remember the fall here — Operation Midway Blitz, the heightened Border Patrol enforcement across the Chicago area, Gregory Bovino parading around the streets with camera crews, the protests at the Broadview processing center — people here were very aware of how impactful it was. It was also happening around the elections, so it was prominent news everywhere and everybody was talking about it.
Over the summer it really died down, and I don’t think people have paid much attention since. ICE has been around all year, but they haven’t been as flashy about it, which has been talked about nationally too. This was a flare-up, and it’s a reminder that it’s still going on even after Bovino left. There have been protests at Broadview this week unrelated to the Evanston incident. So either people are starting to pay more attention as the election gets closer, or the incidents are actually picking up again.
What are the unanswered questions you’re still chasing?
Who were they looking for? Were they actually looking for somebody? That’s been their story — a specific individual — and a lot of people I’ve talked to are really skeptical that’s the case. One witness at the scene told me he felt like they just picked him and drove up on him. Essentially what’s been called a “Kavanaugh stop” — if they’re suspicious of you, they can pretty much find a reason to detain you. And then they dropped it once they realized either that he was a US citizen, which he says he is, or that there were too many people around taking videos for it to be worth their time.
So: What happened in the lead-up, and who specifically were they looking for? 
Afterward, the agents talked to Evanston police — that’s an Evanston police policy; they’re supposed to try to get information from ICE officers. I’ve FOIAed all the body cam footage. I want to see what those conversations were like, and what exactly the agents told police officers when they talked privately.
Part of what we’re trying to do is see the issues that play out from the bottom up rather than the way they get framed nationally. Beyond immigration, is there anything in your coverage that’s shaping local politics more than the national conversation reflects?
The national issues matter to everybody, but they hit communities in completely different ways. Evanston is affluent — college town, Northwestern, wealthier than most suburbs. Affordability is a buzzword that comes up everywhere, but people here talk about it differently.
This is an overwhelmingly progressive Democratic city. Some people in Evanston certainly need it to be more affordable for themselves. But you also have progressive voters saying we want to make Evanston more affordable and more inclusive for other people. Sometimes the affordability conversation gets framed as “life is too expensive for me and we need to make it cheaper for me,” which is true in a lot of places. In somewhere like Evanston, where there are a lot of affluent people who are also very progressive voters, it’s more: If we actually want to say we’re a progressive community, we have to show it. And showing it maybe means building affordable housing.
It’s also a city that passed reparations, which the federal government is challenging right now. That’s going to be a federal court case through the end of this year and probably into next year — the feds challenging the city’s reparations program. That’s something the city prides itself on. Those are big issues here that come out of the national conversation but sound different than how we hear them in national media.

news.title: Judge Tosses Trump Suit Over Iowa Newspaper’s 2024 Poll That Showed Harris Leading
news.text:
An Iowa judge dismissed President Donald Trump’s lawsuit against a pollster and the Des Moines Register newspaper on Sept. 23, finding an inaccurate poll published three days before the 2024 election was protected speech and didn’t violate the state’s consumer fraud law.

The newspaper published Ann Selzer’s poll on Nov. 2, showing Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris leading Trump by 3 percentage points. Trump won the state 56 percent to 43 percent. His lawsuit claimed Selzer acted with “corrupt intent” to help Harris.

The president was joined by U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa state Sen. Brad Zaun, both Republicans, in the lawsuit against Selzer, her polling company, and the newspaper and its parent company. They alleged the misleading coverage diminished their reputations and valuable time and cost them in campaign funds and resources.

The poll also predicted a Democratic victory in Miller-Meeks’s district. Although it did not include Zaun’s race, he blamed the poll’s impact for his loss.

Beattie also found the readers of the Register and Selzer’s polls didn’t suffer a loss.

“Election damages are in any event speculative,” Beattie wrote in the ruling. “It is a claim to have been told the truth. Lying is not fraud, because lying by itself ‘lacks an essential element of a fraud claim: proof of detrimental reliance or actual harm to the plaintiff.’”

The judge also called the case extraordinary, saying that allowing the lawsuit and its claims to proceed could have a “chilling effect” that could discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs.

Beattie said he would have dismissed the case even if he accepted the president’s claims that the poll was intentionally skewed and its results fabricated because the lawsuit did not meet the legal requirements for fraud or consumer deception.

The lawsuit was dismissed with prejudice, permanently closing the case and ending the legal dispute.

Selzer, represented by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), said there was no guarantee the poll was correct.

“Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome,” Selzer said in a statement.

“What we can guarantee is that we will follow the data wherever it leads, even when the results are uncomfortable or unexpected.

“I am grateful that Judge Beattie’s ruling recognizes these principles and reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference.”

FIRE’s chief counsel, Bob Corn-Revere, represented Selzer pro bono.

“We’re pleased that the court recognized what we’ve said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought,” Revere said. “The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of ‘fake news.’”

USA Today Co., formerly known as Gannett and owner of The Register, also called the ruling a “victory for the First Amendment.”

Trump’s personal legal counsel didn’t immediately return a request for comment about the judge’s decision.
news.author: Jill McLaughlin

news.title: MORNING GLORY: El-Sayed might have a problem with the Black vote in Michigan
news.text: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has a problem with a large slice of the state’s Black electorate. It doesn’t like him. That matters in a state where the voting population is 14% Black. (About 2% of Michigan voters are of Arab descent. 1.4% are Jewish.) BLACK VOTERS RIP DEMS OVER TAKING THEM FOR GRANTED IN EL-SAYED'S BACKYARD: ‘HUSH US UP’ In the most recent Washington Post–Schar School poll, Sept. 10–14, only 67% of likely Black Michigan voters supported El-Sayed. A Fox News poll from a month earlier, taken Aug. 6–10, found that 75% of Black Michigan voters said they would vote for El-Sayed. That is a trend in the wrong direction for El-Sayed. Two years ago, then Vice President Kamala Harris carried the Black vote in Michigan with 87%. So El-Sayed is significantly underperforming the most recent Democratic nominee for president. SOCIALIST POLITICIANS ARE 'MORE RACIST THAN THE KKK,' SAYS BLACK DEM OFFICIAL URGING VOTERS TO DITCH EL-SAYED The question is why is El-Sayed so weak with this particular demographic? El-Sayed has addressed this question very directly, including acknowledging that there is mistrust between parts of Detroit’s Black and Arab communities. El-Sayed may already have given up on Michigan’s significant Jewish vote coming around, but on Tuesday he campaigned with former Vice President Kamala Harris at an event aimed directly at Black women. It was an awkward "roundtable" that seemed to have been so narrowcasted at Black women as to have returned right out of peak Woke 1.0, which Congresswoman Alexandra Ocasio Cortez assured us recently is an era behind us. Harris did not get that memo as her remarks Tuesday indicated. "The attack on DEI is an attack on maternal care," Harris opined as an uncomfortable-looking El-Sayed looked on, "including the need to protect Black women in connection with their pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care." The word salad chef of 2024 was back. HARRIS JOINS FORCES WITH RADICAL SENATE NOMINEE IN KEY SWING STATE AS 2028 WHISPERS SWIRL Whether or not the day’s appearance by the former VP helped El-Sayed at all with Black voters won’t be known for some time, but given the numbers in the public polling, El-Sayed had to try something to get Michigan’s crucial voting block at least start thinking about going to the polls in November even if that something was Harris who has been notably absent from the critical Senate races until this week. There is little reason to believe that Harris is the answer to El-Sayed’s core problem. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS LEADERS MUST ADDRESS ‘UNPAID DEBTS’ TO BLACK COMMUNITIES In an August 2026 interview with The Grio, El-Sayed was blunt about the Black-Arab-American divide in and around Detroit: "I think a lot of the mistrust among Black folk in Metro Detroit is well-founded, based on a kind of double standard that too often business owners, particularly in the Arab and, yes, Muslim communities have had when it comes to the way they do business in local communities," El-Sayed said. "You see money go in and then money leaves these communities rather than be reinvested in the community," El-Sayed continued. "It’s a conversation I’ve been having with the Arab and Muslim community for a very long time. We can’t sit here and talk about racism against Arabs and Muslims unless we’re willing to actually look inward and ask how is it that we’re engaging with the Black community in a way that is responsible?" So El-Sayed knows he has a problem with a key demographic. He has tried other approaches before bringing Harris into the state. El-Sayed declared he was open to "reparations" when he appeared with Fox News’ Jesse Watters, saying that an "incredible debt that was put upon black folks as a function of slavery, that we have yet to pay." El-Sayed also told Watters the whole country should be discussing "how do we make people whole." The following month, El-Sayed was talking to leaders of the Black church, saying "unpaid debts" are owed to Black communities, debts that have "long since come due." BLACK CONSERVATIVE REVEALS HOW GOP CAN LOCK DOWN MINORITY VOTERS WITHOUT TRUMP ON BALLOT While the topic of "reparations" polls at 77% approval among Black Americans, only 18% of white voters support the concept. So the more El-Sayed pushes "reparations," the more likely he is to drive off the moderate independents already leery of his radical positions and friendship with Hasan Piker. Then there is the "Trump effect." President Trump collected 13% of the Black vote overall two years ago, and close to 20% of Black men. Does talk of DEI and maternal care at the El-Sayed-Harris roundtable Tuesday bring home votes among Black men? Does chatter about unspecified reparations even drive off the near quarter of the Black population that aren’t signed on to the concept? The long-standing tensions between the Black and Arab-American communities in and around Detroit cannot be resolved in an election cycle that has focused on El-Sayed’s radical break with traditional Democratic campaign themes and profiles. El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, took more than two-thirds of black voters in the primary. Republican nominee Mike Rogers knows this traditional Democratic stronghold is at least partially in play. We can’t see Team Roger’s buy on "urban radio" or in other media serving the Black community, but we have seen Rogers making appearances throughout Wayne County and making many appearances with "Democrats for Rogers" groups featuring Black voters. Everyone knows that El-Sayed and his association with Hasan Piker has driven off the votes of a large number of Jewish Democrats. That the campaign is not connecting with Black voters as it must to give him a shot is the double nightmare for his campaign strategists. What can he do between now and November 3? It is hard to see a path to keep the moderate independent vote even as El-Sayed trots out traditional panders to the Black vote that don’t even resonate as credible or detailed. Even as El-Sayed struggles with basic messaging to core constituencies, Republican groups have poured more than $60 million into the Wolverine state. There are some polls showing El-Sayed with a lead over Rogers outside the margin of error. There were also lots of polls showing him winning the primary against Stevens by double digits, with one memorable miss putting him 18% up in a race he won by one point. The polling doesn’t add up given his problems with the Democratic base. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP So stay focused on El-Sayed’s increasingly frenetic campaign and its sudden lurches here and there. There’s a reason radicals aren’t often nominated by major parties. Both Republican and Democratic Parties are built out of coalitions of interest groups. El-Sayed’s primary campaign fractured the traditional Democratic coalition. There is scant hard evidence that he has found a way to glue it back together again and then motivate it to vote between now and November 3.
news.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's support among Black voters in Michigan is dropping fast, and even a Kamala Harris campaign appearance may not fix the problem.

news.title: ‘Gun-shy’ after 2024: Angie Nixon says Democratic leaders are wary of backing Black women candidates
news.text:
When Angie Nixon got Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer on the phone recently, the Florida Democrat made the ask every candidate puts to their party's leader: Help me fund this race.

His answer, by her account, was noncommittal.

“When I did speak with Sen. Schumer on the phone, it was basically a ‘we will see,’” Nixon said in the latest episode of “Clock It with Symone & Eugene.” “He’s going to look into it. That’s what was said, that he’s going to look into it.”

Nixon, a state representative from Jacksonville, won Florida's Democratic Senate nomination last month in an upset. Her account offers a rare look at how national Democrats are handling a nominee who started as an insurgent, running against the same party establishment that now controls the purse strings.

Nixon and Schumer have yet to have an official meeting in person, though they saw each other last week at an event and spoke. “We are working on a sit-down,” Nixon told MS NOW. “I have talked to some of his staff.”

Asked whether the national party was doing enough to help her win, she was measured but direct: “They could do a lot more.”

Nixon has two explanations for why she believes party leaders are holding back. The first is ideological.

“I am a progressive Democrat, and I am very vocal about putting working-class families first. I am very vocal about progressive values,” she said. “So I think that may be the main issue.”

The second is her race and gender. “Folks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President [Kamala] Harris lost as a Black woman, and so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South.”

A spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee pushed back on Nixon’s criticisms. “We are excited about opportunities to expand the map further and monitor all races closely, including Florida, where Angie Nixon is running an energetic campaign,” they said.

The DSCC has opened a joint fundraising committee with Nixon's campaign, and she attended a fundraiser for it just last week. But it is unclear how much money the DSCC has actually sent to Florida.

A senior Democratic aide with knowledge of the conversations told MS NOW that polling will, of course, help drive spending. Disputing the idea that party leadership is withholding help because Nixon is a progressive, the aide — who was granted anonymity to discuss private conversations — pointed to recent investments in Michigan, where progressive Abdul El-Sayed is the Senate nominee.

The aide also said Democrats have been caught somewhat off-guard as their chances of retaking the Senate have improved sharply in recent months. A map that once had the party playing defense and hoping for the best now requires it to go on offense at a severe financial disadvantage.

That forces hard choices, and Florida may be the clearest example. The simplest explanation for the party's reluctance there may also be the least personal: The state is a reach for Democrats and one of the most expensive in the country to compete in, and every dollar spent there is a dollar that can't go to races that look easier to win.

That calculation has been years in the making. National Democrats have paid less and less attention to Florida as it has shifted from perennial battleground to reliably Republican, and Democratic strategists in the state have long criticized the national party for failing to invest there.

Therein lies the tension.

National Democrats have said for years that they need to compete in every state and every district, especially after losing ground in places like Florida. Nixon argues that her state's reputation as a Republican stronghold is itself a product of her party's neglect. Florida, she said, isn't a “red state; it is an underinvested state.”

Still, the numbers national strategists have to weigh are daunting. Republicans hold an advantage of more than 1.5 million registered voters over Democrats in Florida, according to the state's Division of Elections. No Democrat has won a Senate race there since Bill Nelson in 2012.

Recent polling, though, has been closer than many expected, generally showing a single-point race with Ashley Moody ahead, even as the national environment grows more favorable to Democrats by the day. MS NOW rates the race “likely Republican,” but has it on its list of races to watch.

In late July, the DSCC announced a $40 million investment across 10 states, including Florida. Beyond that, the committee's public posture toward the race has been cautious. After Nixon won the primary, Schumer and DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand issued a joint statement praising her background as a union organizer and criticizing Moody's votes on healthcare. The statement didn't announce any spending.

Even Florida Democrats are tempering expectations. State party chair Nikki Fried has said the party can't necessarily count on a major DSCC investment this cycle.

The financial gap, meanwhile, is wide. Moody raised $11.3 million through the end of July and had $8.4 million on hand after the primary. Nixon raised less than $1 million over the same period.

Some help has trickled in. A DSCC aide, granted anonymity to discuss interactions with the Nixon campaign, told MS NOW that both Gillibrand and Schumer have invested the maximum of $5,000 from their own leadership PACs to Nixon, and added that Gillibrand and Nixon had spoken on the phone. Nixon herself said Gillibrand was “pushing the senators to help support me financially.” But that kind of support won't go far toward closing the gap.

Nixon said she is undeterred.

“They may not be treating it as a competitive race, but I have to continue to prove that it is, and so I am not going to allow that to stop me,” she said. “I know what it is. I know that initially no one is going to really invest in this state, and so I was still able to win [the primary], and so I’m going to work my butt off. That’s all I know.”

For many Democrats, especially Black women, the party's reluctance sends a message of its own. Nixon would be the first Black senator in Florida's history, and she is one of only three Black women who are Democratic Senate nominees this year.

“If people claim to care about Black people, particularly Black women, we are the most consistent members of the Democratic Party that always show up. The state of Florida, we have the second-largest Black population in this country, and so they need to put some respect on our names. What that looks like is go ahead and invest in this state.”
news.author: Sydney Carruth

news.title: Maine’s middle might be swinging to Susan Collins, NYT/Press Herald/Siena poll shows
news.text:
Susan Collins has made a career out of courting moderate Mainers. As she seeks a sixth term in November, new polling shows that game plan is working pretty effectively. 

In the second installment of The New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll of 619 likely Maine voters, conducted Sept. 15 to 22, Collins led her Democratic challenger, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, by three points, 49% to 46%. With the margin of error at 4.8%, the race appears to be neck-and-neck as it enters its final six weeks.

Crucially, in a state where voters have rejected every other Republican in statewide elections since 2014, Collins appears to be pulling voters from the middle.

The Times/Press Herald/Siena poll showed that:

About 13% of Collins voters also said they wanted Democrats to win control of the Senate, and one-tenth said they’d vote for a Democrat for the U.S. House. 

About 12% of voters who said they chose former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election plan to vote for Collins.

Collins has support from 8% of the Democrats surveyed, while Jackson is drawing 3% of Republicans. The candidates were evenly split among independents at 47%.

In the June version of the same poll, which pitted Collins against then-Democratic nominee Graham Platner, Collins was pulling a similar share of Harris supporters, but fewer independents.

Those numbers show Collins might be cobbling together a similar coalition to her last victorious run in 2020, when she won by a 9-point margin. An exit poll conducted that year by CNN found that 13% of Democrats supported Collins. 

The survey was conducted before ProPublica published an investigation about a federal corruption probe into Collins’ 2020 campaign. It’s possible — but far from certain — that the story could hurt her standing with moderates. 

“She has been a leader in the Senate,” said Brian Cashin, a 79-year-old independent voter from Cumberland. “I think Troy would have a tough time making any contribution as a freshman senator and getting on any, you know, committees that would protect Maine and jobs and reverse the tariff situation in Canada.”

Cashin is conservative, but he said he isn’t a straight-ticket Republican voter. He said he would have supported Dr. Nirav Shah if he’d won the Democratic nomination for governor, or had he become the Senate nominee following the withdrawal of Graham Platner.

About 54% of voters said they thought Collins would be a more effective senator than Jackson — including 8% of people who said they would vote for Jackson. Almost 60% said Collins, the chair of the Senate appropriations committee, would bring more resources back to Maine.

Cashin said he’s not thrilled with the president for whom he voted four years ago; Donald Trump’s “shoot from the hip kind of style” on tariffs and the Iran war, he said, has been disappointing.

But he’s among the one-third of voters who said they’d vote for Collins despite their disapproval of her party’s leader. Collins has stood up to Trump enough, especially on tariffs, to earn his vote, he said.

That’s not the case for Molly Hunt.

“(Collins) is supportive of Trump in a vocal way, which I think is unacceptable for anyone in the government at all,” said Hunt, 33, of Biddeford. “Everybody should be against this man, and I think that she rubs shoulders with this guy.”

Hunt, a Democrat, isn’t particularly happy with Jackson, either. The only thing she knows about him, she said, is that he once reportedly threw a water bottle during a disagreement with a fellow lawmaker. He got her vote because she dislikes Republicans’ dismantling of abortion protections and Collins’ crucial 2018 vote for Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

Still, she feels resigned about casting her vote for Jackson. 

“I’m like, I would literally rather have someone throw a water bottle at my head than vote against abortion rights,” Hunt said.

One-third of likely voters feel similarly unenthused, the Times/Press Herald/Siena poll found.

Collins’ supporters are slightly less amped to turn out this November, with about 54% saying they were “very enthusiastic” about their vote, compared to 66% of Jackson’s voters saying so.

But a race this close could well be decided by the small number of voters who shrug their proverbial shoulders before casting a ballot.

Ronald Thackeray said he doesn’t want to vote for Collins, but he will. He agrees with her on many of the issues, but she has spent too long in power, he said.

“The way our government works, I can’t see giving up her position, especially with what they put forward in her replacement,” Thackeray, a 54-year-old independent from Waldoboro, said. “What we’re voting for is garbage. I should have ran for it.”

The New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll of Maine voters was funded with support from the Maine Trust for Local News.
news.summary: Collins is picking up frustrated voters in the middle — those who are less enthusiastic and engaged, but who feel they know the leading Senate Republican well.
news.author: Ethan Horton

news.title: Trump loses big in Iowa court after trying to sue pollster for wrong election call
news.text:
A state judge on Wednesday dismissed a legal challenge Donald Trump brought against The Des Moines Register and its former pollster, rejecting claims that media coverage of a pre-election survey violated Iowa’s consumer fraud law and ruling that press reporting on political contests is fully protected under the Constitution.

Describing the lawsuit as extraordinary, Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie cautioned that letting the case and its "faulty" legal claims move forward in court could have a severe chilling effect that "can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs." 

Judge Beattie ruled in favor of pollster J. Ann Selzer and the newspaper, affirming that political polling and news coverage detailing survey results constitute constitutionally protected political speech rather than a commercial product governed by state consumer protection statutes.

Wednesday's court ruling came just hours after a separate judge held a hearing but did not issue an immediate decision in a legal challenge over Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. Trump barred journalists from the three media organizations last Friday from accessing White House grounds, assailing their news coverage as "fake news."

Following the court ruling in Iowa on Wednesday, a spokesperson representing Trump’s legal team confirmed that the president will take his case forward by appealing the dismissal directly to the Iowa Supreme Court.

Trump originally initiated the lawsuit against Selzer, The Des Moines Register and its parent publishing company in December 2024. The lawsuit accused the defendants of fraudulently publishing deceptive polling data to damage his presidential campaign and aid Democratic candidates, asserting that news coverage of public opinion polls does not constitute protected speech under the First Amendment.

The legal battle in Iowa is part of a broader series of lawsuits filed by Trump and his legal advisers against various media organizations accusing them of political bias. These legal actions have repeatedly called into question the legal boundaries of free speech protections for press organizations, though some of those cases have previously resulted in out-of-court settlements.

The free speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression took on Selzer's legal defense. Speaking on Wednesday, Selzer said she was grateful for the ruling, which she noted "reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference."

"Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome," Selzer added in a written statement.

Attorneys representing Selzer at FIRE and her fellow co-defendants also celebrated the favorable court ruling.

"Today is a victory for the First Amendment — and for the essential role of a free press in American democracy," Polly Grunfeld Sack, chief legal counsel for USA Today Co., said in a statement celebrating the outcome. USA Today Co., formerly known as Gannett, is the parent company that owns The Register.

In his decision dismissing the legal challenge, Beattie wrote that Trump’s lawsuit attempted to "stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability." After hearing the legal arguments, the judge concluded that constitutional protection "is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed."

Beattie said the lawsuit would still have to be dismissed even if, solely to decide the pending defense motions, he accepted the Trump team’s claims that the poll was deliberately skewed and its results fabricated. "Even with this assumption, each of the three counts still fails," the judge wrote, explaining that the lawsuit failed to meet the legal requirements for fraud or consumer deception.

The disputed survey, conducted by Selzer’s firm in the final days of October and published just days before Election Day 2024, showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democratic presidential nominee, capturing 47% support among likely Iowa voters to Trump’s 44%. Trump ultimately won Iowa by securing 56% of the nearly 2 million votes cast.

Republican U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa state Sen. Brad Zaun had joined Trump as co-plaintiffs in the lawsuit.

Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun had alleged in their legal filing that the misleading poll coverage harmed their public reputations, consumed valuable time in the final days of the campaign, and depleted significant campaign funds and resources.
news.summary: A judge on Wednesday dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit accusing The Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race

news.title: Trump’s ‘Election Interference’ Lawsuit Against Des Moines Register Tossed by Iowa Judge
news.text:
An Iowa judge dismissed President Donald Trump’s lawsuit Wednesday against the Des Moines Register and pollster J. Ann Selzer over a 2024 Iowa poll that inaccurately showed then-Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris leading Trump in the state.

Selzer’s poll, released days before the 2024 election, predicted Kamala Harris would win the key swing state of Iowa; Trump went on to win the state by 13 percentage points. The president sued Selzer the Des Moines Register and Gannett in December, a month after he beat Harris in the election. Selzer, a veteran pollster who has her work consistently cited by media outlets, had a “significant and impactful opportunity to deceive voters” with her incorrect poll, Trump’s initial lawsuit claimed. The lawsuit also said the poll “was not reality, it was election-interfering fiction.”

Polk County District Judge Scott Beattie granted motions to dismiss filed by Selzer and Selzer & Company, as well as the Des Moines Register and its parent company, Gannett Co., in a ruling issued Wednesday. 

Trump’s team alleged violations of the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act, fraudulent misrepresentation and negligent misrepresentation. The plaintiffs also sought to prevent the defendants from publishing additional allegedly deceptive polls.

In his ruling, Beattie said the plaintiffs’ claims attempted to turn constitutionally protected speech into legal liability. “At its core, the Plaintiffs’ Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability,” he wrote. “The case must therefore be dismissed.”

Beattie ruled that the poll and the Register’s reporting on it constituted protected political speech under the First Amendment. He rejected the plaintiffs’ argument that the poll should be treated as commercial speech because it was commissioned and published by for-profit companies.

“Election polling is speech protected by the First Amendment, both because it involves a conversation between a pollster and a voter and because the poll itself is speech,” the judge wrote. He added that reporting on the poll during a presidential and congressional election year was “speech about a matter of public concern, occupying the summit of the pyramid of First Amendment values.”

The judge also said that the fact that a poll turned out to be inaccurate did not, by itself, make it a provably false statement of fact under the legal standards applicable to the case.

“A poll is simply an estimate,” Beattie wrote. “A poll reports responses from a sample of voters and includes a reported margin of error.” He characterized polls as “snapshots with margins of error” concerning an election that had not yet occurred.

“A statement of conjecture about a future state of affairs is not provably false, even when the speaker is alleged to have known better,” he wrote.

Selzer was defended pro bono by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), a free speech advocacy group. 

“We’re pleased that the court recognized what we’ve said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought,” FIRE Chief Counsel Bob Corn-Revere, who led Selzer’s defense, said in a statement. “The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of ‘fake news.’ That may work for him as a campaign slogan, but it is not a thing in the law.”Representatives for Trump did not immediately respond to TheWrap’s request for comment.

The dismissal was entered with prejudice, meaning the claims cannot be refiled in the same form. The court also denied the plaintiffs’ request to enjoin the publication of future polls.
news.summary:
Judge Scott J. Beattie sided with the newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer over an inaccurate 2024 Iowa poll between Kamala Harris and Trump

news.title: Support for California's Wealth Tax Is Shrinking
news.text:
The California wealth tax will be on the ballot this November. In order to pass it, supporters need to get one vote more than 50 percent of the total votes cast. And for a while it appeared they were cruising to victory with some polls showing the tax running at +19. However, more recent polls show the race is tightening.

A proposed tax on billionaires is faltering in California, according to a new poll by POLITICO and its partners, with public support dropping off as opponents launch a massive advertising blitz.Fewer than half of likely voters (45%) said they would vote for the tax on the assets of California’s wealthiest residents, while 43% said they would vote against it and 12% were undecided, according to the UC Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll. That’s down from February, when proponents of the measure, Proposition 40, held an edge.“The trend in Prop 40 is certainly going against Prop 40,” said Jack Citrin, a University of California, Berkeley, political science professor and co-director of the poll. “From a historical point of view, you’d think the no side are gaining and would potentially win.”

Another recent poll was better for the tax but still well below the edge shown in earlier polls.

Proposition 40, which was proposed by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West as a way to fill massive funding gaps triggered by President Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, has the support of 52% of likely voters in the latest survey from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan research group in San Francisco. It found 42% of likely voters said they’d oppose the measure and 2% were undecided.

But even the news in this poll doesn't look so good when you look at the competing measures that are on the ballot. In California, if the features of two different ballot initiatives conflict, only the one which passes by the largest amount goes into effect. The other ones are effectively locked out, even if they passed. With this in mind, opponents of the tax have put two rival initiatives on the ballot.

Prop. 41, which the poll found was supported by 51% of likely voters, would require the state auditor to review proposed special taxes before they’re placed on the ballot and invalidate taxes that don’t comply with the state spending limit. Prop. 42 would prohibit new state personal property taxes, including those on retirement accounts and assets. It had support from 54% of likely voters in the PPIC poll. Both measures are supported by Building a Better California, a new group with major funding from Google co-founder Sergey Brin.

So Prop 41 is within one point of Prop 40, which is basically a tie. Prop 42 is leading Prop. 40 by two points. If either of those two get a higher vote tally, then Prop 40 is dead even if it passes. So at this point it looks like a tossup.

But there's also reason to think the numbers for Prop 40 will continue to sink. That's because Sergey Brin has put a lot of his own money behind defeating it while the union pushing the tax has no war chest at all. The campaign to defeat 40 has only just gotten underway but already there are signs it is working.

A resounding 83% of likely voters said they had heard some or a great deal about the measure — a remarkably high number given that the main opposition committee only launched its first ad in late August. Likely voters who said they’d heard a “great deal” were opposed by a 57-38 margin.“The campaign is just starting, and roughly a gazillion dollars are going to be spent on it,” said Jon Cohen, founder and CEO of TrueDot, whose firm fielded the poll. “The fact that the people who are the most tuned in are the most opposed points to significant vulnerability that I think the yes side has.”

Not unlike Kamala Harris, the more people hear about the wealth tax, the less they like it. And they are going to hear a lot about it between now and November. In particular, it seems that voters are turned off when they hear that this might not be a one-time tax as the proponents have promised. A recent anti-Prop 40 ad states, "when the money runs out, Sacramento will be back with yet another tax." 

And that's not a political trick; it's absolutely true. There is no plan for what to do when the first glut of other people's money runs out. Some of the proponents have already hinted that a repeat of the tax might be the next plan. So you either commit to driving all the billionaires out of the state or you should stop this now before the state gets used to spending money it does not have.

The wealth tax isn't dead yet but there are signs it could be headed for defeat. That's probably the best thing that could happen to this state, even if two-thirds of Democrats are too dumb to know it.

news.title: Michigan student confronts El-Sayed over Iran stance in tense exchange: ‘Do you stand with us?’
news.text: A Michigan student confronted Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed about his position on Iran during a town hall Wednesday, invoking his family's stated persecution by the Iranian regime before repeatedly pressing the candidate on whether he stood with Iranians opposing the government. Iman Dashti, who identified himself as Persian, told El-Sayed during a town hall at the University of Michigan that members of his family had suffered under Iran's government. "My cousin was hunted in the streets of Iran by the IRGC because her hijab wasn't on right," Dashti said. He also alleged that her uncle was sentenced to death and received 50 lashes under the Iranian government. ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS Dashti then confronted El-Sayed over leaked audio from earlier this year in which he said he did not want to comment on the death of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei because "there are a lot of people in Dearborn who are sad today." "That silence had a gaping hole in our community," Dashti told El-Sayed Wednesday. Dashti asked El-Sayed whether he regretted that silence, whether he would renounce people who held vigils supporting Khamenei and whether he stood "unequivocally against the IRGC" and the Islamic Republic of Iran. El-Sayed responded by arguing that the United States has too often acted as "the world's policeman" while saying he supported movements for democracy and freedom abroad. AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS "One can disagree with the governance of a foreign country. One can stand in solidarity with freedom and democracy movements," El-Sayed said. He went on to reject U.S.-led regime change in Iran. "I will always stand for and with democratic movements always," El-Sayed said. "But I also don't believe that we were in the right to go to war to topple the government of Iran. It was not our responsibility to do. It is the responsibility of the people of Iran to decide what their leadership should look like." Dashti pressed him again. "You stand with us?" he asked. "I will always stand with movements for freedom and democracy," El-Sayed responded, before again warning against U.S. involvement in regime change. "We should not be in the business of regime change," he said. El-Sayed added moments later, "I want freedom and democracy for the people of Iran, no question. But I want that to be done by the people of Iran, coming together as a community to decide how to create democratic change in their society." Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for additional comment on the exchange and attempted to reach Dashti through Instagram. El-Sayed, who won Michigan's Democratic Senate primary in August, is running against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The contest has drawn substantial national attention and spending. The Iran confrontation was one of several notable exchanges during Wednesday's "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall at El-Sayed's alma mater. KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN While discussing public health infrastructure, El-Sayed appeared to make a prediction about the party and the gender that will win the White House in 2028. "I'm looking forward to working with the next Democratic president when she takes office in 2029," El-Sayed said, adding that he hoped to work with that administration to modernize the nation's public health infrastructure. El-Sayed did not identify whom he had in mind. His remarks came as former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democrat presidential nominee, returned to Michigan to campaign with El-Sayed. Harris has not announced a 2028 presidential campaign. El-Sayed also criticized President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance during the event. "Donald Trump and JD Vance can't seem to keep my name out their mouth," El-Sayed said. "They don't really know how to say it, though, which is fine, because I believe in teaching opportunities." Trump and other national Republicans have repeatedly targeted El-Sayed during the midterm campaign, while El-Sayed has responded by criticizing the president. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "As he noted in his response, Abdul will always stand with movements for freedom and democracy, and he condemns government anti-free speech violence," Roxie Richner, El-Sayed's campaign spokesperson, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Abdul has also been clear that the United States should not be in the business of spending our tax dollars abroad on regime change wars that take our service members’ lives, waste our tax dollars and raise our prices. He believes American taxpayer dollars are best spent here at home to invest in infrastructure, education and healthcare."

news.title: Iowa judge dismisses Trump’s lawsuit against Des Moines Register and pollster (World)
news.text:
Iowa judge dismisses Trump’s lawsuit against Des Moines Register and pollster

Trump’s lawsuit tossed

A judge on Wednesday dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit accusing The Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race, rejecting the president’s claim that the newspaper’s poll coverage violated Iowa’s consumer fraud law.

Calling the case extraordinary, Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie said that allowing the lawsuit and its “faulty” claims to proceed could have a chilling effect that “can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs.” He sided with pollster J. Ann Selzer and the newspaper in affirming that the poll and coverage of it were constitutionally protected political speech, not a commercial product.

The ruling Wednesday came hours after a judge heard arguments but did not rule from the bench in a case on Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. Trump banned the three outlets last Friday, assailing what he called “fake news.”

After the ruling in Iowa Wednesday, a spokesman for Trump's legal team said the president will take his case to the Iowa Supreme Court.

Trump filed the lawsuit against Selzer, The Des Moines Register and the newspaper’s parent company in December 2024, accusing them of fraudulently publishing inaccurate poll results to damage him and help Democrats, saying coverage of polls is not protected speech.

Trump and his team have filed several lawsuits against media organizations accusing them of bias, calling into question the boundaries of free speech protections, particularly for the press. Some of those lawsuits have ended in settlements.

Selzer’s case was taken up by the free speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression. She said Wednesday she was grateful for the ruling, which “reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference.”

“Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome," Selzer said in a statement.

Selzer's attorneys at FIRE and her co-defendants also celebrated the ruling.

“Today is a victory for the First Amendment — and for the essential role of a free press in American democracy," Polly Grunfeld Sack, USA Today Co. chief legal counsel, said in a statement. USA Today Co., formerly known as Gannett, owns The Register.

In dismissing the case, Beattie wrote that Trump’s lawsuit sought to “stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability.” After hearing the arguments, the judge concluded the constitutional protection “is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed.”

Beattie said the case would have to be dismissed even if, solely for the purpose of deciding the motions, he accepted the Trump team’s allegations that the poll was intentionally skewed and its results fabricated. “Even with this assumption, each of the three counts still fails,” the judge wrote, because the lawsuit did not meet the legal requirements for fraud or consumer deception.

The poll, conducted by Selzer’s company in the final days of October and released just days before Election Day 2024, showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democrats’ presidential nominee, capturing 47% of Iowa likely voters, to Trump’s 44%. Trump ultimately won the support of 56% of the nearly 2 million Iowans who voted.

U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa state Sen. Brad Zaun, both Republicans, had joined Trump’s lawsuit.

Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun alleged the misleading coverage diminished their reputations, valuable time in the final days of the campaign, and campaign funds and resources.
